title: Robot Hands Are Learning to Feel!
summary: Have you ever tried to pick up a delicate cookie without breaking it? Your fingers feel how hard to squeeze. Robots struggle with that because most don't have a sense of touch. But that's changing! A company called DAIMON Robotics has created a special sensor that fits on a robot's fingertip. It's packed with over 110,000 tiny sensing points — like having super-sensitive skin. This lets the robot feel textures, slipperiness, and how hard it's gripping something. To help robots learn faster, DAIMON built a giant collection of data, called Daimon-Infinity. It's the world's largest dataset for robot touch, with millions of hours of information from over 80 real-world tasks — like folding clothes or working on a factory line. They even shared 10,000 hours of it for free so other scientists can use it. Prof. Michael Yu Wang, the company's co-founder, says that giving robots a sense of touch is crucial. "Data scarcity remains a primary bottleneck in robot learning," he explains. By combining touch with vision and language, robots can understand the world more like we do. In the future, touch-enabled robots might work in hotels, convenience stores, or help at home. So next time you see a robot, imagine it one day being able to feel a high-five!
why_it_matters: When robots can feel, they might one day help us with chores, assist older people, or work in hospitals—making everyday life easier and safer.

background_read: DAIMON Robotics (a company that builds advanced robot hands) has created a sensor that acts like super-sensitive skin for robots.
For a long time, robots could see and hear but not feel—so picking up a delicate cookie without breaking it was almost impossible.
A huge collection of touch data called Daimon-Infinity now teaches robots how to handle things gently, using millions of hours of practice from tasks like folding clothes.
Article_Structure: WHO: DAIMON Robotics and co-founder Prof. Michael Yu Wang.
WHAT: They built a fingertip sensor with over 110,000 touch points and the world's largest touch dataset.
WHERE: At DAIMON Robotics' labs (exact location not given in the article).
WHY: To give robots a sense of touch so they can learn faster and do delicate jobs in homes, stores, and factories.

perspectives.description: Engineers see touch as the missing piece that will finally let robots handle soft, fragile objects and work right next to people.
Some people worry that even touch-smart robots could be too expensive or might still make mistakes, delaying their use in real homes.
